blocks.title:
A history of measuring time
Measuring the time in a year or a day has always been a priority
blocks.instruction: Complete the notes. Use NO MORE THAN ONE WORD for each answer.
content: People in ancient civilisations had sophisticated {{31}} to record the passing of time
Stonehenge: a 5000-year-old stone circle in England
- It was possibly built by druids (priests)
- The stones seem to have been erected for viewing the {{32}} on the solstice (the longest day of the year).
In the past, days were divided into 12 periods
- Shadow clocks have been discovered in {{33}} which consisted of a large column
- Some were constructed out of {{34}} and were several metres in height
- These were used in various locations and had moving parts
- However, they were ineffective in {{35}} conditions. Engineers in China addressed this problem by using mercury and {{36}} of water instead.
- The first known one was constructed in Germany in the 10th century
- In the 14th century, a clock with a {{37}} to mark the hours was constructed; this is still in Salisbury Cathedral, England
- Clockmakers aimed to produce clocks that were {{38}} and able to tell the time more precisely, especially to aid sailors with navigation
- Thomas Tompion, an English clockmaker, managed to produce a clock that was small enough to be {{39}}.
- Tompion gave one of these to an English {{40}}.
